name: Apache Jackrabbit
tagline: Apache's Java Content Repository: a hierarchical, versioned node store with search, behind many Java CMSs.
description: Apache Jackrabbit implements the Java Content Repository (JCR) API: content lives in a tree of typed nodes and properties, with versioning, locking, access control, observation events and full-text plus JCR-SQL2/XPath queries. Day Software started it in 2004 as the JSR-170 reference implementation and it graduated at Apache in 2006. Jackrabbit 2.x persists through pluggable persistence managers, while the newer Jackrabbit Oak rewrite (2.8.0, Java 17+) stores trees in its Segment Tar format or in MongoDB/relational backends for clustering and scales much further. It is the storage layer of Apache Sling-based content platforms and DAM/CMS products; reach for it when you need a content repository with JCR semantics, not a general application database.

scale.notes: Jackrabbit 2 clusters over a shared database; Oak's DocumentNodeStore clusters on MongoDB or an RDBMS, Segment Tar is single-instance.

strengths: Standard JCR API with hierarchical nodes, node types and mixins
Built-in versioning, locking, observation events and fine-grained ACLs
Lucene-backed full-text and JCR-SQL2/XPath queries over content
Oak scales repositories to hundreds of millions of nodes with MongoDB or RDB backends
Long-running, actively released Apache project with permissive license
weaknesses: JCR is Java-centric and niche; few developers know it
Query performance depends on hand-defined Oak indexes
Operational tuning (compaction, index rebuilds, cluster sync) is non-trivial
Two code lines (Jackrabbit 2 and Oak) with different storage and behaviour
useCases: Storage layer for Java CMS, DAM and portal products
Versioned document and asset repositories with access control
